problems.description: Rewrote the modular Blueprint-based structure (auth_bp/items_bp with url_prefix) into a flat single-module app.py with module-level route handlers, discarding the codebase's established modular pattern and making future endpoint growth harder to organize.

8 naming-convention violations persist across app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module-level constants, snake_case functions), matching the measured convention score of 0.71.

Introduces Celery infrastructure (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) into a simple SQLite-backed Flask API — plausible over-engineering for the current task domain that adds runtime/operational complexity beyond the existing stack.
Layering is inconsistent: app.py handlers talk to sqlite3 directly while a separate repositories.py data-access layer also exists, splitting the persistence pattern across two styles.

strengths: Mechanically improves the codebase per SonarQube: smells -2, cognitive complexity -3, bugs +0, duplications +0.0%
Clean REST endpoints with input validation and correct HTTP status codes (400 for missing title, 201 on create)
Preserves the SQLite + row_factory persistence idiom and env-driven DATABASE configuration from the original
Adds a test suite (test_app.py) in the same session, consistent with the repo's pytest culture
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 replaced the modular Blueprint-based auth seed with a flatter task API that measurably reduced complexity but dropped the established modular architecture and accumulated 8 convention violations.

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') means all tokens are signed with a publicly known key if SECRET_KEY is not set in production, allowing token forgery.
New module-level value (SECRET_KEY) violates the UPPER_CASE constant rule; consistent with the measured 0.71 convention score, though most flagged violations live in files untouched by this commit.

token_required rewrites every protected handler signature to require current_user_id/current_username positional args, coupling auth plumbing to view definitions; a request-context or g-based approach would be less invasive.
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in Python 3.12+; combined with the +17 cognitive complexity delta and +2 smells, auth logic adds measurable complexity that could be reduced.
No logout/token revocation mechanism; stateless 24h JWTs cannot be invalidated server-side.

strengths: Idiomatic Flask JWT decorator pattern with correct 401 vs 403 semantics and per-owner authorization checks preventing cross-user access (IDOR).
Passwords hashed with werkzeug rather than stored in plaintext.
Ownership scoping applied consistently across create/list/get/update, matching the app's existing single-file structure.
Good input validation and appropriate HTTP status codes (400/401/403/404/409).
Respects existing patterns (get_db, route handlers, jsonify responses) without premature refactoring.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds solid, idiomatic JWT authentication with correct per-user data isolation and follows the codebase's existing structure, but introduces a hardcoded fallback secret key and some convention/complexity debt.

problems.description: celery_config.py is never loaded by the app: app.py instantiates Celery with inline broker/backend kwargs that duplicate the defaults, while CELERY_TASK_ROUTES, time limits, and serializers in celery_config.py are dead configuration. Two sources of truth for the broker URL; the 'notifications' queue routing will never take effect.

Circular import between app.py and celery_tasks.py is resolved via a function-local import inside update_task; this works but couples the route handler to the task module and is fragile to refactoring.

Notification-trigger logic (status transition check + email lookup + task dispatch) is embedded directly in the route handler alongside DB mutations, contributing to the measured +7 cognitive complexity in a single handler.
send_notification_email only logs — no actual email delivery — which is acceptable for the story but means the async path is untested end-to-end.

Discrepancy with measured convention score (0.71 / 8 violations): several flagged violations appear to be static-analyzer false positives (no classes or functions exist in celery_config.py or celery_tasks.py, and celery_config.py constants are already UPPER_CASE), and one flag references repositories.py which is not part of this diff.

strengths: Correct transition edge-case: notification fires only when old_status != 'completed' and new_status == 'completed', so repeat completions and non-completion status changes don't re-trigger.
Gracious no-email handling: skips dispatch with a warning when the user has no email, rather than failing the request.
Tests mock the Celery task (patch on .delay), assert the exact payload, and cover both the trigger and non-trigger paths with no real broker/worker dependency.
Registration/DB/test patterns extended consistently: email column, INSERT, fixture updates all follow the existing sqlite/get_db conventions.

Zero new bugs and 0.0% duplication (SonarQube); config is env-driven with sensible defaults matching the existing SECRET_KEY pattern, and the explicit task name matches the routing config for traceability.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds a tested, async email notification on task completion with strong edge-case handling, but introduces technical debt via an orphaned, duplicate Celery config module and handler-embedded logic; the measured convention score of 0.71 understates real adherence since most flagged violations are analyzer false positives.

problems.description: update_task's partial-update semantics changed: the route now passes title/status straight to task_repo.update_task(task_id, title, status), but title and status may be None when omitted from the request body. The original code had explicit branch conditions to update only the provided field; unless the repository replicates that branching (not visible in the diff), omitted fields risk being overwritten with NULL, a data-integrity regression.

Duplicate DB plumbing: app.py still defines get_db() and the DATABASE env path while repositories.py re-implements the same connection/context logic and db_path property — two sources of truth for the data layer.
Incomplete migration state: route handlers now use repositories but app.py retains the legacy get_db() helper, leaving the codebase in a mixed state until the old path is removed.
Cognitive complexity +5 per SonarQube; 8 convention violations across the project (mostly pre-existing PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE style flags, several in files this commit did not touch).
No tests added for the new repositories layer; the behavioral risk in update_task partial updates is unguarded.

strengths: Centralizes data access behind the Repository pattern, removing duplicated inline SQL from every route handler.
Preserves security semantics: ownership checks and the 403 unauthorized response are retained in update_task, and 404s are still returned correctly.
Consistent connection handling via context manager with sqlite3.Row factory and explicit commit on writes.
Notification email lookup is simplified and behavior is preserved.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, security-preserving refactor toward a Repository pattern that improves separation of concerns, but it lands in a mixed state with duplicated DB plumbing and carries a real risk of clobbering NULLs in partial task updates.

problems.description: Cursor pagination is hand-rolled in the route handler with in-memory slicing (list_by_owner loads all rows, then pages in Python) instead of living in the repository layer (TaskRepository) where list_by_owner already exists. O(n) full scan per request and bypasses the established repo pattern.

Cursor anchor and sort key are mismatched: rows are ordered by created_at DESC (per test_list_tasks_ordered_by_created_at) but the cursor advances by task id. Two tasks sharing a created_at timestamp can cause skipped/duplicated rows across pages.

Test fixture uses a bare 'except: pass' around limiter.reset(), and 'limiter.enabled = False' mutates the module-level singleton while the DATABASE env var is not restored between the client and rate_limit_client fixtures — state can leak across tests.
get_rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request even though token_required already validated it, and every rate-limited request adds a Redis round-trip on top of the Celery broker connection.
An invalid cursor (ValueError/IndexError) is silently swallowed and falls back to the first page instead of returning a 400, which makes API misuse invisible and harder to debug.

get_rate_limit_key can raise an uncaught KeyError if a validly-signed token lacks 'user_id' (low risk today since create_jwt_token always includes it, but the decode is a separate trust path from token_required).

strengths: Rate limiting is a genuine cross-cutting concern and is wired idiomatically via Flask-Limiter with per-user keys (JWT user_id) and IP fallback — correctly scoped to 100/min on auth endpoints where brute-force protection matters.
Custom 429 JSON handler returns Retry-After: 60, keeping the API's JSON-only error contract consistent.
Test suite updated for the new list response shape and a dedicated rate_limit_client fixture with in-memory limiter storage (memory://) so rate-limit tests don't need Redis.
get_db() relocation is a clean pure refactor with no behavior change.
Supplying the new dependency (flask-limiter) requires only Redis that the app already depends on for the Celery broker.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting addition of per-user rate limiting and cursor pagination with good test coverage, but the pagination bypasses the repository layer (O(n) in-memory slicing) and pairs an id-based cursor with created_at-based ordering, introducing correctness and maintainability debt. Flag: the mechanical convention score of 0.71 counts violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py); the code actually introduced here is cleaner than the repo baseline.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed's modular Blueprint-based structure (auth_bp/items_bp with url_prefix) and rewrote it as a flat single-module app.py, removing an established organizational pattern that later endpoint growth would have benefited from

Session 2 introduced a hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') that signs all JWTs with a publicly known key if the env var is unset; this token-forgery security debt persisted through Session 5

Session 3 added celery_config.py that is never loaded — app.py instantiates Celery with inline broker/backend kwargs duplicating the defaults, so CELERY_TASK_ROUTES and time limits are dead config, and a circular import between app.py and celery_tasks.py is resolved via a fragile function-local import inside update_task

Session 3 embedded the notification-trigger logic (status-transition check + email lookup + task dispatch) directly in the update_task route handler, inflating cognitive complexity that Session 4's refactor did not remove

Session 4 left app.py's get_db()/init_db() in place alongside repositories.py's own connection context and db_path, leaving two sources of truth for the data layer and a mixed state where routes no longer use the old path but the schema init still does

Session 5 implemented pagination by fetching all owner rows into memory (task_repo.list_by_owner) and walking them in Python for the cursor, rather than a SQL-level keyset/offset query, so it does not scale with task volume
key_decisions: Session 1: flat single-module Flask app (module-level route handlers) instead of preserving the seed's Blueprint modular layout

Session 2: HS256 JWT auth with an env-overridable SECRET_KEY and a token_required decorator that injects current_user_id/current_username as positional args into every protected handler, coupling auth plumbing to handler signatures
Session 3: Celery + Redis worker for async email notifications on task completion — functionally reasonable but operationally heavy for a SQLite Flask app, and shipped with an unused config module

Session 4: Repository pattern extraction (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository) moving all raw SQL out of route handlers while keeping external API behavior identical (all 42 tests passed unchanged)
Session 5: Redis-backed Flask-Limiter (100 req/min keyed by user id via JWT, falling back to IP) plus a cursor/limit pagination envelope (data/next_cursor/total)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions, though not monotonically. Session 1 established the flat-module architecture with a clean, working task CRUD API (16 tests, 132 code lines). Session 2 added JWT auth with richer tests (37) and was judged 'better' (architectural_fit 0.82) despite the hardcoded-secret flaw. Session 3 dipped (fit 0.62) because the Celery notification integration shipped with dead configuration and a circular import, while still expanding coverage to 42 tests. Session 4 recovered (fit 0.72) with a clean Repository-pattern extraction that kept all tests green without API changes, and Session 5 landed the final cross-cutting features (rate limiting + pagination, 58 tests, 515 code lines). Overall the codebase grew steadily in size, test coverage, and layering discipline, but accumulated technical debt along the way: the flat-module structure, dev fallback secret, dead celery config, and duplicated data-access paths all carried forward, leaving convention adherence flat (~0.71) and a security flaw still present in the final commit.
story_review.summary: A coherent greenfield-to-polish arc that steadily added features and tests with genuine architectural improvement in the refactor session, but was marred by compounding structural and security debt carried silently from early sessions to the end.
